title: Growing in Virtue: One Psychological Perspective
description: Nicolas-Henri Jacob, from Bourgery’s “ Traité complet de l'anatomie de l'homme,” 1831–1854, via Wikimedia Commons . In this article, I want to focus on a psychological framework developed by psychologists for thinking about the more general process of growth in virtue. This framework encourages attention to (1) motivation, (2) mindset, and (3) means. What orients us to grow in virtue? Do we think such growth is possible? And if so, how can we actually grow? I present this as a general framework that can apply in many particular cases. Motivating Growth Motivation here is, on the surface, fairly straightforward. If we are to grow in virtue or character, we must desire to grow in that way. Motivation might arise from a recognition that one is focused on avoiding vice more than on pursuing virtue. For instance, thinking to oneself when faced with a challenge—I don’t want to make a mistake—rather than thinking about what the best thing one might do is. We might think about motivation to grow in virtue by asking ourselves two questions: (1) What is the good that I want to grow in my capacity to realize? and (2) What are the fears and competing desires that inhibit that growth? If we can appropriately address the inhibitory fears and desires, we will be more free to pursue growth. This is what growth in temperance and fortitude often is. Even more, the good that we want to grow in is ideally an expression of our desire for justice—we recognize that we ought to be better for God and others. Mindset Mindset is about our beliefs, especially regarding our psychology and the way the world works.

title: What is it to Seek and Speak the Truth in Love?
description: Welcome to part two of my five-part series on Intellectual Charity. The first part is here , though it isn’t necessary that you read it before you read this entry. In all areas of life, the Christian is called to the moral heights: turn the other cheek; go the extra mile. We are called to emulate Christ, who laid down his life for us while we were still at enmity with him. We hear parables that encourage us to go above and beyond the call of duty. Indeed, the technical term for such an act—an act that goes above and beyond the call of duty, like when a stranger saves a dying man found on the side of the road, taking him to an inn and paying for it with his own money—is supererogation , a word that comes to us from St. Jerome’s Vulgate translation of our Lord’s parable of the Good Samaritan. As the Samaritan says to the innkeeper, whatever more you spend ( supererogaveris ), I will repay you. So, it should be no surprise to us, then, that in seeking and speaking the truth, we Christians are called to a high standard. But what exactly is the standard? Just how high is it? Remember when Peter asked how many times he had to forgive his brother? You can hear him thinking he’s got a pretty high bar already when he says “seven.” And honestly, that is pretty high, isn’t it? Seven times for the same type of sin?! But recall our Lord’s answer of seventy -seven, or even seventy times seven. Is the bar for seeking and speaking the truth equally audaciously high? title: Time in Science and Philosophy
description: Johannes Vermeer, “The Astronomer,: 1668, via Wikimedia Commons. Physicists who work in general relativity carry two very different definitions of time in their research. One is “proper” time, which is a measure of the amount of physical change that a system experiences. Proper time is what a clock measures. Carry a clock from event A to event B, and the number it displays is a direct observable that you can write down. A series of events for a given object is called its worldline. I might awake, drive into work, sit for four hours, drive to an airport, take a plane to the East Coast, and check into a hotel. My worldline has involved a series of events in which I am alternately stationary, moving at constant speed, accelerating, and rising a certain distance away from the center of the Earth. But the clock I take with me will display an elapsed time which anyone who reads it—even though they moved on a different worldline-- will agree upon. “Coordinate” time, on the other hand, is one of four coordinates assigned to events in the four-dimensional continuum called spacetime. Spacetime consists of three space-like dimensions and one time-like dimension in our universe. The path of any material entity through spacetime can be visualized as a series of events, which are linked together to form its world line. Coordinate time is a labeling of events that allows one to quantify the relationship between different worldlines. For example, if I play a three-minute song on my iPhone while on a plane, and an observer on the ground wants to know how long the song lasted by her reckoning, she must first assign times to the start and end events in her stationary reference frame, correcting for the travel time of the wireless signal from my airplane.
